Part D · Chapter 3

Predicting the next token

A probability for all tokens, three settings that change the draw, and the loss used to train it

A language model gives a probability to all possible next tokens. This chapter shows those probabilities for GPT-2 small (MIT licence), computed offline, on invented SharkCam messages. Then it covers temperature, top-k and top-p sampling, the generation loop, the context window, the cross-entropy loss that trains the model, and perplexity, which can mislead across languages.

The Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish texts have not yet been checked by a native speaker.

You will need: softmax and temperature and cross-entropy (0.7), tokens (D1), embeddings (D2) and the slope p − y (A3).

A score per token

Guess first. GPT-2 has read “Found a young grey bamboo shark in a rock pool at Juhu at low tide. Length 44 cm, dark bands across its back. We photographed it and put it”, and the true next word is “back”. How much probability do you think the model gave to “back”, and was it the model’s first choice?

A language model takes the tokens so far, the context, and gives a probability to all possible next tokens. GPT-2 small, a language model with 124 million weights, first computes one score z per token, 50,257 in all. Softmax then turns the scores into probabilities p that add up to 1. A higher score gives a higher probability, and p depends only on the differences between scores.

  1. The rows are the 14 likeliest next tokens (▁ marks a leading space), with the score z, relative to the top score, and a bar for the probability. Click the row ▁back, and the boxes below the bars work out its 17%.
  2. Choose the context “Capital of a state” and the top token ▁Maharashtra gets 67%. Choose “An open sentence” and the top token ▁water gets 34%, so more tokens share the rest.
tokenscore zprobability (bar)

For “put it”, GPT-2 small gives ▁in 27%, ▁back 17% and ▁on 13%, so the true next token came second.

How it works

Take ▁back after “put it”, whose score is z = −0.45. Then, with e = 2.718, e−0.45 = 0.638. The sum of ez over all 50,257 tokens is 3.73, so p = 0.638 / 3.73 = 0.171, the 17% of its bar. The top token ▁in has z = 0, so p = e0 / 3.73 = 1 / 3.73 = 0.268.

\(z_k\)score of ▁back: −0.45→\(e^{z_k}\)numerator: 0.638÷\(\sum_j e^{z_j}\)sum over all 50,257 tokens: 3.73=\(p_k\)probability of ▁back: 0.171

We use ez because it is positive for all scores, however negative, and it grows as z grows. Dividing by the sum makes the 50,257 probabilities add up to 1. Adding the same number to all scores multiplies the numerator and the sum by the same factor, so p does not change. This is why the figure shows scores relative to the top one, with 0.0 for the top token. The readout “effective number of choices” is defined under Go deeper.

Common belief. A language model looks up the sentence it has stored and returns the next word.

Why it fails. GPT-2 small has no table of sentences to look up. It computes 50,257 scores from its weights, and after “put it” its top token was “in”, not the true “back”.

Better account. The model is a function from a context to a probability distribution over tokens. It was fitted to a large body of text, so its probabilities reflect that text.

Quick quiz

Two tokens have scores 0 and −0.45. If all other tokens are ignored, what are their probabilities?

e0 = 1 and e−0.45 = 0.638, which sum to 1.638. So p = 1 / 1.638 = 0.61 and 0.638 / 1.638 = 0.39. Only differences between scores matter.

All 50,257 scores are raised by 2. What happens to the probabilities?

They do not change. ez+2 = e2 × ez, so the numerator and the sum are both multiplied by e2, and the factor cancels.

What the figure shows

Scores are relative to the top token, so the top one reads 0.0 and the others are negative. The rows are the 14 likeliest next tokens, which together have 92% of the probability for “put it”. The last row adds up the other 50,243 tokens. The mark ▁ means a leading space (see the tokenisation chapter). Scores and probabilities are from GPT-2 small, computed offline.

Entropy and the effective number of choices

The entropy \(H = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k\), in nats, measures how spread out the probabilities are: it is small when one token dominates. Its exponential eH, the effective number of choices, is the number of equally likely tokens that would give the same entropy. For “put it” it is 13.8, close to the 14 of a fair die with 14 equal faces. For “Mumbai is the capital of the Indian state of” the answer “▁Maharashtra” gets 67% and the effective number of choices drops to 4.3. For the open sentence “The shark was swimming in the” it is 89.

Two contexts to look at

In “Two milk” the true next token is “▁sharks”. GPT-2 gives it a probability near 0.01%, rank 635 of 50,257, and puts milk crates, bottles and tanks first. A likely reason is that milk sharks are rare in its training text, although the figure cannot show the cause. The Hinglish line (m13) has an effective number of choices of 1,238. GPT-2 has probably seen little text spelled this way, which would explain why its preference is so flat. The probabilities describe what GPT-2 learned from its text. They do not record what is true.

More questions

The effective number of choices is 4.3 for one context and 1,238 for another. In which context is the probability concentrated on fewer tokens?

In the first. A small number means the probability rests on a few tokens.

Where this is used

Used in: all assistants (D7). The next section shows how a token is chosen from these probabilities.

Temperature, top-k and top-p

Guess first. You must pick the next token from a distribution. If you always take the most likely one, what happens to a report that should read “about fifty” one day and “about twenty” the next? And what might a slider named temperature do to the probabilities?

Greedy decoding always takes the likeliest token, whereas sampling draws a token at random, with chances equal to the probabilities. Temperature T divides the scores before softmax: T below 1 sharpens the distribution, and T above 1 flattens it. Top-k keeps the k likeliest tokens. Top-p keeps the fewest likeliest tokens whose probabilities add up to at least the top-p setting. In both cases the kept probabilities are rescaled to add up to 1.

  1. Choose “Message m01: about” and press Draw 200 at T = 1. The top token ▁50 has only 3.8%, so the outlines show draws spread over many tokens.
  2. Move T to 0.5 and ▁50 rises to 8.7%. Move it to 2 and the top token falls to 0.9% while the row of the other 50,243 tokens rises to 90%.
  3. Set T back to 1 and Top-p to 0.9, and Tokens kept reads 86. Choose “Message m02: put it” and it reads 12.
tokenscore zpale: at T. solid: after the cuts. outline: draws

A higher T moves probability from top tokens to unlikely ones, and top-p 0.9 keeps 86 tokens at T = 1 for “The biggest was about” against 12 for “put it”.

How it works

Take ▁back after “put it” at T = 0.5, where its score z = −0.45 becomes −0.45 / 0.5 = −0.90. Then e−0.90 = 0.407, and the sum of ez/T over all 50,257 tokens is now 1.905, against 3.73 at T = 1, so p = 0.407 / 1.905 = 21.3%. The sum shrinks because dividing by 0.5 doubles the size of all negative scores, while ▁in, with z = 0, rises from 27% to 52%.

▁backscore z = −0.45÷ 0.5 =−0.90z / T at T = 0.5→ e−0.9 =0.407numerator÷1.905sum over all 50,257 tokens=21.3%probability at T = 0.5

Dividing by T scales all the gaps between scores by 1/T. A T below 1 widens the gaps, so the top token gains probability, and a T above 1 narrows them, so the unlikely tokens gain. The order of the tokens never changes, only how steeply the probability falls with rank.

Common belief. A higher temperature makes the model more creative, and a lower one makes it more accurate.

Why it fails. Temperature has no access to facts, and it only flattens or sharpens the model’s own probabilities. At T = 2 more draws are tokens that the model rated unlikely, so errors become more likely. At T near 0 it repeats its single favourite, which can be wrong too.

Better account. Temperature trades variety against reliability for one model, and a better answer needs a better model.

Quick quiz

Probabilities are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. What does top-p = 0.7 keep, and what are the new probabilities?

It keeps the first two tokens, since 0.5 alone is below 0.7 and 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8 reaches it. They are divided by 0.8: 0.625 and 0.375.

Why can a high temperature produce odd words even when the model is good?

At T = 2 the tokens outside the top 14 have 90% of the probability for “The biggest was about”. Flattening gives these tokens, which the model itself rated unlikely, a larger chance of being drawn.

Trying the figure

Start with the context “The biggest was about”, the one before the 50. Press Sample one token a few times at T = 1, then press “Draw 200”. The sampled tokens differ from press to press, because the model has no strong favourite (the top token has 3.8%). When a draw falls in the group of tokens not shown, the figure names a token from a small stored sample of them, since the 50,243 tokens are not listed one by one. Now move T down to 0.3 and draw again. The draws come mostly from the tokens shown, because the other 50,243 tokens now have 16%. Move T up to 2 and most draws come from the 50,243 tokens not shown, which now have 90%, so the sampled words look strange. Pick the context “Message m02: put it” to see a sharper case. There T = 0.5 lifts ▁in from 27% to 52%. At T = 2 the top token has 3.9%, and the tokens not shown have 77%. The cumulative curve under the bars shows how many tokens the cut-offs keep.

As T falls towards 0, the highest-scoring token (if one score is highest) takes all the probability, and as T grows without limit, all tokens become equally likely.

Top-k and top-p in four contexts

Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps as many as needed to reach the setting, so it adapts. With top-p at 0.9, the clear question about Maharashtra keeps 5 tokens, “put it” keeps 12, “The biggest was about” keeps 86, and the Hinglish line keeps 3,336. A fixed top-k of 40 would keep 40 tokens in all four cases. Holtzman and colleagues (2020) proposed top-p, which they call nucleus sampling, to cut off the unreliable tail while keeping variety. Fan and colleagues (2018) used top-k sampling. Many libraries, and this figure, apply temperature first, then top-k, then top-p, and renormalise.

The equations

\[ p_k \;=\; \frac{e^{z_k/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j/T}} \qquad\qquad S_p \;=\; \text{the fewest tokens, likeliest first, with } \sum_{k \in S_p} p_k \;\ge\; p \]

  • \(z_k\) is the score of token \(k\), \(V\) is the vocabulary size (50,257), \(T\) is the temperature and \(p_k\) is the probability of token \(k\) (0.7). As \(T\) grows towards infinity all tokens become equally likely. As \(T\) falls towards 0 the top token takes all the probability.
  • \(S_p\) is the set that top-p keeps, and the \(p\) in it is the threshold you choose, such as 0.9. The threshold is a different number from the probability of one token. After the cut, the kept probabilities are divided by their sum, so they add up to 1 again. Top-k keeps the \(k\) tokens with the largest \(p_k\) and renormalises the same way.

In Python

The code below does the same with eight of GPT-2's scores for “put it”. It ignores the other 50,249 tokens, so its probabilities (32% for ▁in) differ from the figure's (27%).

import numpy as np

tokens = [" in", " back", " on", " to", " into", " up", " down", " out"]
z = np.array([0.0, -0.45, -0.70, -1.17, -1.32, -1.75, -1.92, -2.21])   # GPT-2 scores for "...and put it"

def probs(z, T=1.0, k=None):
    z = z / T
    if k is not None:                          # top-k: keep the k largest scores, drop the rest
        cut = np.sort(z)[-k]
        z = np.where(z >= cut, z, -np.inf)
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())                    # subtract the max so it cannot overflow
    return e / e.sum()

for T, k in [(1.0, None), (0.5, None), (2.0, None), (1.0, 3)]:
    print(f"T={T}, k={k}:", probs(z, T, k).round(3))

rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
draws = rng.choice(len(tokens), size=1000, p=probs(z, 1.0, 3))
print({tokens[i]: int((draws == i).sum()) for i in range(3)})
print("greedy:", tokens[int(np.argmax(z))])
T=1.0, k=None: [0.318 0.203 0.158 0.099 0.085 0.055 0.047 0.035]
T=0.5, k=None: [0.531 0.216 0.131 0.051 0.038 0.016 0.011 0.006]
T=2.0, k=None: [0.212 0.17  0.15  0.118 0.11  0.089 0.081 0.07 ]
T=1.0, k=3: [0.469 0.299 0.233 0.    0.    0.    0.    0.   ]
{' in': 442, ' back': 295, ' on': 263}
greedy:  in

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Temperature 0 divides by zero. Many libraries treat it as greedy decoding, which is the limit as \(T\) falls to 0. If two runs with the same settings differ, you drew random numbers without fixing the seed. If top-p keeps too few tokens, remember that it works on the probabilities after temperature has been applied.

Where this is used

Used in: the temperature slider of the hallucination figure in D7, the settings page of a chat assistant, and the loop of the next section.

The generation loop

Guess first. A language model predicts one next token at a time. How would you use it to write a whole report of 30 tokens, and what goes into the model at step 2?

A language model writes a text one token at a time by repeating a loop. In one step the model gives a probability to all possible next tokens. One token is drawn from them with the temperature and cuts of the sampling section. The loop adds the drawn token to the end of the text. That longer text is the input of the next step, and a model that reads its own earlier output in this way is called autoregressive. The loop stops when the end token is drawn, which ends the text, or when a maximum length is reached.

  1. The figure uses a tiny model whose tokens are words: its table counts which word followed a given pair of words in 500 made-up reports. Choose the start “we found a”, and the bars show its probabilities for the word after “found a”: young 58%, small 25% and big 17%.
  2. Press Next token. The drawn word joins the text in coral, and the two underlined words were the model’s whole context for that draw.
  3. Press Run. It stops when [end] is drawn or the text reaches 40 words.

The text so far (the underlined words are the model's whole context)

Next-word probabilities, given

wordcountpale: at T. solid: after cuts

Natural log of the model's probability for the drawn words (the small numbers)

The loop is the same for GPT-2 and for this tiny model; only the model changes.

How it works

Follow the loop from the start of a report. At T = 1 the probability of a word is its count in the table divided by the total count for that context. Of the 500 reports, 163 begin with “we”, so p(we) = 163 / 500 = 0.326. If “we” is drawn, the input of step 2 is the start marker, a symbol before the first word, and “we”. The table has only one continuation for that input, “found” (163 of 163). After “found a” the table gives young 95 / 163 = 0.583, small 41 / 163 = 0.252 and big 27 / 163 = 0.166.

0.326p(we)×1p(found | we)×1p(a | we found)×0.583p(young | found a)=0.190probability of “we found a young”→−1.66ln of it: −1.12 + 0 + 0 − 0.54

The probability that the model gives to a whole text is the product, over its tokens, of the probability of a token given the tokens before it. Its natural logarithm is the sum of the logarithms, which are the small numbers under the drawn words in the figure. The model reads its drawn words as if a person wrote them, so an unlikely draw changes the input of all later steps.

Analogy. Writing with a phone keyboard that offers three suggestions, tapping a suggestion again and again.

Where it breaks. The keyboard offers a few words and you choose, whereas a language model scores all 50,257 tokens (GPT-2) and a random draw chooses.

Quick quiz

At step 2 of the loop, what is the model’s input?

The original prompt plus the token drawn at step 1, which is a text one token longer.

Why does the loop stop?

The model draws the end token, or the text reaches a maximum length such as the context window.

Running the figure

Press Next token a few times. A press does one turn of the loop. It looks up the last two words, turns the counts into a distribution, applies the temperature and cuts, draws a word and appends it. Press Run to watch a whole report. Change the temperature and run again, or press “New random seed” to get a different report from the same settings. In 300 runs from the empty start, T = 0.2 gave about 175 different reports and T = 1.6 gave about 260, and the counts change a little with the random seed. Many steps have only one possible next word: in the table, 67% of the 15,287 counted word positions (words and end marks) follow a two-word context with a single continuation, and a temperature cannot change a draw that has one option. A model with 50,257 possible tokens leaves far more choices at most steps, as the sampling section showed.

From one draw to the loss of a text

The average of the small numbers under the chips, with the sign flipped, is the loss of the text, and its exponential is the perplexity (see the last section and the Part 0 chapter on cross-entropy). GPT-2’s loop is the one described by Alammar (2019). The output token joins the input and the model runs again. This goes on until it draws the end token or fills its 1,024 tokens.

The model behind the figure

The model behind the figure is a table of word-triple counts from 500 made-up reports (14,787 words, 92 different words), with a context of two words. It is a counting model with no neural network in it. The counts are in tiny.json. The figure gives a word the score ln(count / largest count for that context), so softmax at T = 1 returns count / total count, and temperature and the cuts work as in the sampling section.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If generated text repeats the same few words, look at the settings first. A temperature near 0 or a top-k of 1 makes the model follow its single favourite again and again.

Where this is used

Used in: the transformer's generation step and the KV cache (D5), where the loop is made fast.

The context window

Guess first. A diver’s report of 46 tokens begins “Morning dive report. Tag 4127 was a small bamboo shark” and ends “The shark in the Juhu rock pool was tag”. If the model could see only the last 20 tokens, would it still give a high probability to the number 4127 coming next?

A language model can use only the tokens inside its context window, the largest number of tokens it reads at once (1,024 for GPT-2 small). When a text is longer than the window, the software that calls the model usually cuts off the oldest tokens. Those tokens then have no effect on the model’s output.

  1. Press Show all 46. The model reads the whole report of 46 tokens and gives 42% to ▁4, the start of 4127.
  2. Drag the slider down to 42 tokens and the probability is still 21%. Press Cut off the tag, which gives 41 tokens: the word “Tag” is struck through and the probability falls to under 0.1%.

With all 46 tokens GPT-2 small gives 42% to ▁4, the start of 4127, and with 41 tokens, which leave out the word “Tag”, it gives under 0.1%.

How it works

Count the window from the end, so that a window of w tokens contains the last w tokens of the 46. The word “Tag” is token 5, so the smallest window that contains it has 46 − 5 + 1 = 42 tokens. A window of 41 tokens starts at ▁4, so the number 4127 is still inside it but “Tag” is outside. The probability of ▁4 falls from 21% to under 0.1%.

1,024 ÷ 117window ÷ Hindi report m05=8reports fit: 8.75 rounded down|1,024 ÷ 23window ÷ its English meaning=44reports fit: 44.5 rounded down

The window is counted in tokens, so a language that needs more tokens for the same report fits fewer reports into it. Hindi report m05 takes 117 tokens under GPT-2 and its English meaning takes 23, as the tokenisation chapter showed.

Common belief. A chat model remembers the whole conversation.

Why it fails. The model reads only what is inside its window. A chat application usually sends the earlier turns again along with a new message. When the conversation grows past the window, the application may cut the oldest turns or replace them with a summary, so the model never receives the cut text.

Better account. The window is where the model reads the current conversation, and what it learned in training is in its weights. If a reply depends on something from the conversation, that text must be inside the window.

Quick quiz

Why does the probability fall between 42 and 41 tokens and not gradually?

The word “Tag” occurs once, as token 5. A window of 42 tokens is the smallest one that contains it, and a window of 41 leaves it out. The two windows differ only by that word, so the fall happens in one step.

How many reports of 59 tokens fit in a window of 1,024 tokens?

The quotient 1,024 / 59 is 17.4, so 17 reports fit, because part of a report does not count.

Reading the window slider

The probabilities are from GPT-2 small, computed offline: the same prompt is shown to the model one window at a time. Slide the window down from 46 tokens. The probability of the first token of the tag is between 21% and 42% from 46 down to 42 tokens. At 41 tokens, where the word “Tag” drops out, it is about 0.01% (0.0001 in the data), and it is under 0.1% for all shorter windows. At 41 tokens GPT-2’s top guess is “ged” (32%), which would make “tagged”. The cliff is sharp because the tag appears once. The data show the drop but not its cause. A likely reason is that the closing word “tag” points back to the earlier word “Tag”, which the number followed. A usable window is longer than this toy one, but the rule is the same: tokens outside it have no effect on the output.

Window size and cost

GPT-2’s window is 1,024 tokens long (Radford et al., 2019). The window is counted in tokens, so the cost of languages returns (see the tokenisation chapter). A longer window costs more, because attention compares all pairs of tokens (see the chapters on self-attention and long context).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model seems to ignore the start of a long prompt, count its tokens before anything else. Check whether your library cut the text from the left or from the right. Cutting from the wrong end removes the instructions or the question.

Where this is used

Used in: sparse and linear attention, which stretch the window (D6), and test-time training, which tries another way to remember (D6).

Training with cross-entropy

Guess first. For the true token ▁back the model gave 17%. We need a number that is small when the model gave the true token a high probability and huge when it gave almost none. What would you compute from the 17%?

The loss of one token is ℓ = −ln p, where p is the probability the model gave to the true next token and ln is the natural logarithm. It is near 0 when p is near 1 and large when p is near 0, and its unit is the nat. Training a language model lowers the average of this loss over a huge amount of text.

  1. Press One training step. The true token ▁back rises from 17% to 35%, and the loss, shown to three decimals, falls from 1.767 to 1.055.
  2. Read the boxes. A step subtracts the step size η (1 on the slider) times the slope from a score. For ▁back the slope is p − 1 = −0.829, so its score rises from −0.45 to 0.38. For the rival ▁in, the likeliest wrong token, it is p = 0.268, so its score falls from 0 to −0.27.
  3. Press Reset, then Ten steps. The loss is 0.108 after ten steps, and hovering over step 4 of the curve shows 0.307.
tokenscore zprobability

For ▁back after “put it”, the loss starts at 1.77 nats (p = 17%) and, at step size 1, falls to 0.31 after four steps and 0.11 after ten.

How it works

Take ▁back after “put it”, for which the model gave p = 0.171. Then ℓ = −ln 0.171 = 1.77 nats.

▁backtrue token:0.171 − 1 = −0.829slope \(p_k - y_k\)→−0.45 − 1 × (−0.829) = 0.38new score|▁instrongest rival:0.268 − 0 = 0.268slope \(p_k - y_k\)→0 − 1 × 0.268 = −0.27new score

In symbols, ℓ = −ln py for the true token y, and the slope of ℓ at the score zk of token k is \(p_k - y_k\). Here yk is 1 for the true token and 0 for all others. This is the slope of the softmax classifier in the logistic-regression chapter. Subtracting η times the slope raises the true token’s score and lowers the other scores in proportion to their probabilities, the strongest rival most. The figure changes the scores directly, whereas a full model changes its weights, so the scores of other contexts move too.

Common belief. A language model is trained for the right answer, so counting correct predictions is the measure.

Why it fails. There is usually no single right next token, since after “put it” both “in” and “back” are fine. Counting only hits would give no credit for the 17% given to “back”, and no slope to improve it.

Better account. Cross-entropy gives credit for any probability put on the true token, and it has a slope at all scores.

Quick quiz

The true token has p = 0.9 before a step. What is the slope of the loss at its score?

p − 1 = −0.1. It is small because the model is nearly right. A model with p = 0.01 would have a slope of −0.99.

Why does the slope at a wrong token’s score equal its probability?

The label yk for a wrong token is 0, so \(p_k - y_k = p_k\). A likely wrong token is pushed down hard, and an unlikely one hardly at all.

Terms

loss of one token \(\ell\)

The training step in detail

The update subtracts η times the slope from all scores. The slope of the loss at the true token’s score is p − 1, which is negative, so its score rises. The slope at any other token’s score is p, which is positive, so those scores fall, the strongest rival most. This is the slope p − y that the logistic-regression chapter found for a softmax classifier (A3) and that backpropagation uses at the output of a network (B4). The step sizes and the average over many examples come from B3 and B5. Pretraining uses a very large number of such examples, with the true next token at all positions of all texts.

A whole text, and teacher forcing

The loss for a whole text with \(n\) tokens is the average over its positions. The model scores all positions in one pass, using the true earlier tokens as context. This is teacher forcing, and one pass then gives \(n\) training examples.

\[ \ell_t \;=\; -\ln p(x_t \mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}) \qquad\quad L \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \ell_t \qquad\quad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k} \;=\; p_k - y_k \]

  • \(x_t\) is the \(t\)-th token of the text and \(\ell_t\) is the loss at position \(t\). \(L\) is the mean loss over the \(n\) positions.
  • \(p(x_t \mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\) is the probability the model gave to token \(x_t\) after the tokens before it.
  • \(p_k\) is the probability of token \(k\) and \(y_k\) is 1 for the true token and 0 for all others (the one-hot label of A3). The slope is \(p_k - 1\) for the true token and \(p_k\) for the rest.

Three values of the loss

p = 0.171▁back after “put it”→1.77−ln p, nats|p = 0.0001▁sharks after “Two milk”→9.21−ln p, nats|p = 1/50,257a uniform guess→10.82ln V, the starting loss

The starting loss

A model that starts with all scores equal gives all tokens \(1/V\), so its starting loss is \(\ln V = 10.82\) for GPT-2’s vocabulary. Training brings the average well below that. If the first loss of a new run is far from \(\ln V\), something is probably wrong (B8).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A loss of inf or nan often means \(-\ln 0\) was computed. Compute the loss from the scores with a function such as log_softmax or cross_entropy, which does not form a zero probability. Also check the first loss against \(\ln V\).

Where this is used

Used in: pretraining of all models in this part, and fine-tuning (D7).

Perplexity, and its trap

Guess first. When GPT-2 reads the same report in English and in Hindi, in which language is its loss per token higher, averaged over the tokens?

Perplexity is eL, where L is the mean loss −ln p over the n tokens of a text. It is comparable only for the same tokenizer and the same text, so it can mislead across languages.

  1. Choose m02, the report on Tag 4127 in English. The shaded tokens show their loss in nats, and the readout gives mean loss 5.03 and perplexity 152.9.
  2. Choose m06, the same report in Hindi: 227 tokens, mean loss 2.07 and perplexity 7.9.
  3. Press Total loss, nats and then Bits per character. The order reverses, with m02 lower than m06 in both.

Per token GPT-2 small gives the Hindi report a perplexity of 7.9 and the English one 152.9, but the total loss is 469 nats in Hindi and 201 in English.

How it works

Take the Tag 4127 report in English (m02) and in Hindi (m06). The totals of −ln p over their n tokens are 201.2 and 469.3 nats, and dividing by n gives the mean loss L.

201.2total, m02÷40tokens n=5.03mean loss L→e5.03 = 152.9perplexity|469.3total, m06÷227tokens n=2.07mean loss L→e2.07 = 7.9perplexity

In symbols, \(\mathrm{PPL} = e^{L}\) with \(L = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_t \ln p_t\), and if a model gave all tokens the probability \(1/N\), then PPL \(= N\), so perplexity reads as an effective number of choices. Bits per character is the total loss in bits (nats divided by ln 2) per character. The characters of a text are the same however it is cut into tokens, so bits per character can be compared across tokenizers. For these two reports it is 4.4 for Hindi and 1.9 for English. These numbers describe GPT-2 on these invented texts, not Hindi as people write it.

Common belief. A lower perplexity means a better model, whatever it is compared with.

Why it fails. GPT-2’s perplexity per token is 7 to 10 on the Hindi and Marathi reports and 105 to 187 on the English ones, although the total loss is higher in Hindi. The per-token number depends on how the text is cut into tokens.

Better account. Compare perplexity only for one tokenizer and one text; otherwise use total loss or bits per character.

Quick quiz

A 4-token text has true-token probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.1 and 0.8. What is the perplexity?

The losses are 0.693, 1.386, 2.303 and 0.223, which sum to 4.605. The mean is 1.151, and e1.151 = 3.16. The model does as well as one that gives the true token the probability 1/3.16 at all four positions.

With one tokenizer and text, model A has perplexity 20 and model B 25. Which has the lower mean loss?

Model A. Its mean loss is ln 20 = 3.00, and model B’s is ln 25 = 3.22.

Terms

perplexity
\(e^{L}\), the exponential of the mean loss; the number of equally likely tokens that would give the same mean loss
bits per character
the total loss in bits divided by the number of characters, so that texts cut into tokens in different ways can be compared

Why the Hindi report looks easy per token

Pick a Hindi message and look at the shaded tokens. GPT-2 splits a Devanagari letter into bytes (see the tokenisation chapter), and the figure shows these byte pieces as �. Most letters become two pieces. The first piece is the two lead bytes, which say that a Devanagari letter is coming. The second piece is the last byte, which says which letter it is. The figure does not label the two kinds. Pairing the pieces in order, a lead piece followed by a last-byte piece, gives these averages. About 31% of the Hindi and Marathi tokens have a loss under 1 nat, against 8% of the English ones. In the eight Hindi and Marathi messages the lead pieces cost 1.1 nats on average and the last-byte pieces cost 3.0 nats, and about 46% of the 1,438 tokens are lead pieces. These cheap pieces bring the average down, which gives a perplexity of about 8 for a report whose total loss is higher than that of its English version. In these messages the English tokens cost 4.9 nats on average and the Hindi and Marathi tokens cost 2.1. The Hindi report costs more in total because it needs more tokens, and the pieces that identify a letter cost 3.0 nats on average. Switch the chart to total loss and to bits per character to see this.

The report in four languages

All sixteen messages are invented. Take the report on Tag 4127. In English (m02) it has 40 tokens and a total loss of 201 nats, a mean loss of 5.03 and a perplexity of \(e^{5.03} = 152.9\). In Hindi (m06) it has 227 tokens and a total loss of 469 nats, a mean loss of 2.07 and a perplexity of 7.9. Per character, the English report scores 1.9 bits and the Hindi one 4.4 bits. Across the sixteen invented messages, the perplexity per token is 7 to 10 for Hindi and Marathi and 105 to 187 for English. For the Tag 4127 report the total loss is 201 nats in English, 359 in Hinglish, 469 in Hindi and 523 in Marathi. Jurafsky and Martin note that the perplexity of two language models is only comparable if they use identical vocabularies. Radford and colleagues (2019) avoid the issue. They divide the total log-probability by the number of canonical units of a data set, such as words. A language model’s perplexity is a good number for comparing two versions of one model on one text. It says little across tokenizers.

The equation

\[ \mathrm{PPL} \;=\; e^{L} \;=\; \exp\!\Big(\!-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\ln p_t\Big) \;=\; \Big(\prod_{t=1}^{n} p_t\Big)^{-1/n} \]

  • \(p_t\) is the probability the model gave the true token at position \(t\), and \(L\) is the mean loss of the previous section.
  • If a model gave all tokens the probability \(1/N\), then \(L = \ln N\) and the perplexity would be \(N\). So perplexity reads as an effective number of choices.

Check before reuse

Check before reuse. The Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish texts have not yet been checked by a native speaker. The numbers show how GPT-2 treats these texts. They do not show how well it reads Hindi or Marathi as people write them.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Before you compare two perplexities, check that both come from the same tokenizer and the same text. If they do not, compare total loss or bits per character.

Where this is used

Used in: checking pretraining runs (B8) and the perplexity of a reply in D7.

More questions

Why can Hindi text have a lower per-token perplexity than English under GPT-2?

Many Hindi tokens are byte pieces of a letter, and the lead pieces have a low loss (1.1 nats on average). They lower the average without showing that the model reads Hindi well.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory Three tokens have scores \(z = (0, -0.45, -0.70)\). Compute their probabilities at \(T = 1\) and at \(T = 0.5\). Which token gains, and by how much?

    Hint

    Divide the scores by \(T\) first, then exponentiate, then divide by the sum.

  2. theory A distribution is 0.50, 0.25, 0.10, 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01. What does top-k with \(k = 3\) keep and what are the new probabilities? What does top-p with \(p = 0.9\) keep? Which of the two would keep more tokens if the distribution were flat?

  3. theory A model gives the true tokens of a text the probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.1 and 0.8. Compute the loss of the tokens, the mean loss and the perplexity. Explain the perplexity as a number of choices.

  4. theory Show that for softmax and \(\ell = -\ln p_y\) the slope at the score \(z_k\) is \(p_k - y_k\). Then compute the slopes for the true token (\(p = 0.171\)) and for the rival ▁in (\(p = 0.268\)) in the figure.

    Hint

    Write \(\ell = -z_y + \ln\sum_j e^{z_j}\) and use the chain rule (0.6).

Practice

  1. practice Write top_p(probs, p) in NumPy. Test it on the distribution of Theory 2, draw 1,000 samples with seed 4127, and compare the counts with the renormalised probabilities.

  2. practice Load loss.json. Per message, compute the mean loss, the perplexity, the total loss and the bits per character. Reproduce the chart. Which language has the lowest perplexity and the highest total loss?

  3. practice Load tiny.json. Write next_dist(w1, w2, T), then generate five reports at \(T = 0.5\) and five at \(T = 1.5\) with a fixed seed. Compute the perplexity of the reports under the model at \(T = 1\).

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam may use a language model for three jobs. One fills a catch report from a template, one suggests a follow-up question to a fisher, and one reads a tag number out of a message. Which decoding settings would you pick for these jobs, and why? What would you measure to check your choice?

  2. open After “Two milk” GPT-2 gave “sharks” 0.01%. How could you make a language model useful for SharkCam's own messages? Name two approaches, say what these need, and say what could go wrong.

    Hint

    One option changes the prompt, and another changes the weights (see B7 and D7).

  3. open Design a fair way to say how well a model reads Hindi compared with English. What would you use in place of per-token perplexity? Could your measure still be unfair to one language?

Come back later

Try these after two days, and again after a week, without looking back.

The Hindi report m05 takes 117 GPT-2 tokens and its English meaning 23. About how many times more does attention cost for the Hindi report, if cost grows with the square of the length? (Chapters D1 and 0.2)

The ratio of lengths is 5.1, so the cost ratio is about \(5.1^2 \approx 26\).

Softmax scores are (3, 3, 3). What are the probabilities, and what does a temperature of 0.1 change? (Chapter 0.7)

One third for all three. Equal scores stay equal at any temperature, because only differences between scores matter.

The true token has a probability of 0.9. What is the slope of the loss at its score, and at the score of a wrong token with p = 0.05? (Chapter A3)

\(p - 1 = -0.1\) for the true token, and \(+0.05\) for the wrong one. Both are small because the model is nearly right.
